profile.summary: AIDO.RNA is a family of RNA foundation models from GenBio AI; its Hugging Face repositories and current code use the name GB.RNA. The models read an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and turn it into embeddings that a downstream model can use, for tasks such as RNA secondary structure prediction, mRNA-related prediction and RNA function prediction. The largest model has 1.6 billion parameters and was trained on 42 million non-coding RNA sequences.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The models are encoder-only transformers pretrained with a masked language modelling (MLM) objective: parts of the sequence are hidden and the model learns to predict them. The 1.6B model has 32 layers, hidden size 2,048, feed-forward size 5,440 and 32 attention heads, with a vocabulary of 16 tokens. The 650M model's configuration has 33 layers, hidden size 1,280, intermediate size 3,392 and 20 attention heads. Both configurations use rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU activations. Users normally adapt a backbone to a task through GenBio's ModelGenerator framework, which offers embedding, sequence-level and token-level classification, and regression heads.

sections.body: The repository documentation lists seven RNA backbones: gb_rna_1b600m, gb_rna_1b600m_cds, gb_rna_650m, gb_rna_650m_cds, gb_rna_300m_mars, gb_rna_25m_mars and gb_rna_1m_mars. GB.RNA-1.6B and GB.RNA-650M were trained on non-coding RNA. GB.RNA-1.6B-CDS and GB.RNA-650M-CDS are domain-adapted versions for coding sequences, whose Hugging Face metadata name the base models. The three MARS models were trained on 886 million RNA sequences from the MARS database. The Hugging Face repositories read are named GB.RNA rather than AIDO.RNA, and the sources read do not explain the difference. The model cards call the backbones aido_rna_1b600m and aido_rna_650m, while the pinned repository uses gb_rna_ names. A result should name the checkpoint, its Hugging Face revision and the backbone name used; this page read GB.RNA-1.6B at revision cea90e53 and GB.RNA-650M at revision efaf4af4.

profile.summary: BiRNA-BERT is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction tasks. It can read a sequence either one nucleotide at a time, for fine-grained tasks such as secondary structure prediction, or as compressed byte-pair tokens, so that long RNAs can be processed without cutting them short. It is a 117M-parameter transformer encoder trained on about 36 million non-coding RNA sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; model card opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BiRNA-BERT is a BERT-style transformer encoder trained with the MosaicBERT framework. It uses ALiBi relative positional encoding instead of fixed position embeddings, which lets it handle sequences longer than those seen in training. Its main idea is dual tokenisation: the same model is trained by masked language modelling on both byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokens, with a vocabulary of 4096, and single-nucleotide (NUC) tokens. BPE compresses long sequences so they fit in memory, while nucleotide tokens keep the per-base detail needed for tasks such as secondary structure prediction. With the released tokenizer, an unspaced sequence is split into BPE tokens and a space-separated sequence into nucleotide tokens.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The main checkpoint is buetnlpbio/birna-bert, used with the tokenizer buetnlpbio/birna-tokenizer. The paper also trained BPE-Only-BERT and NUC-Only-BERT as controls, and the buetnlpbio account lists bpe-only-rna-bert and nuc-only-rna-bert. The README warns that the current version is substantially updated and suggests re-analysing data processed with earlier versions. The README's own embedding example loads a different model name, Lancelot53/birnabert-2ep, while the model card loads buetnlpbio/birna-bert; the sources do not explain the difference. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision (this page read revision 35bceaf6) and say whether BPE or nucleotide tokenisation was used.

steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import transformers
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-tokenizer")

config = transformers.BertConfig.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-bert")
mysterybert = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("buetnlpbio/birna-bert",config=config,trust_remote_code=True)
mysterybert.cls = torch.nn.Identity()

# To get sequence embeddings
seq_embed = mysterybert(**tokenizer("AGCTACGTACGT", return_tensors="pt"))
print(seq_embed.logits.shape) # CLS + 4 BPE token embeddings + SEP

# To get nucleotide embeddings
char_embed = mysterybert(**tokenizer("A G C T A C G T A C G T", return_tensors="pt")) 
print(char_embed.logits.shape) # CLS + 12 nucleotide token embeddings + SEP
PY

profile.summary: DNABERT is a DNA language model that applies the BERT approach from natural language processing to genomic DNA. It reads a DNA sequence of up to 512 tokens, split into k-mers, and is pretrained on the human genome by predicting masked k-mers. Users fine-tune it with a small labelled data set to predict features such as promoters, splice sites and transcription factor binding sites, and can inspect its attention to find motifs and score variants.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT adapts the BERT language model to DNA. A sequence is cut into k-mers, each base joined with the bases that follow it, and these k-mers become the tokens. During pretraining on human genome sequences, the model sees contiguous spans of k-mers masked (about 15% of the input, raised to 20% for the last 20k of 120k steps) and learns to predict them, so it learns general patterns of DNA from unlabelled data. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned with a small labelled data set for a specific task. The repository adds tools to visualise attention, find motifs and score the effect of sequence variants with a fine-tuned model.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 2.1, 2.2.2; README: sections 5 to 7

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are four pretrained checkpoints, one for each k-mer size from 3 to 6, with the same architecture and settings. The paper reports results with k = 6 because it performed best, and says k = 3 to 6 gave very similar results. The README's download links have expired and point users to the Hugging Face copies. A result should name the k-mer size and the Hugging Face revision; this page read DNA_bert_6 at revision c56e67ea. The repository extends code from Hugging Face transformers and its README sets up a Python 3.6 environment with CUDA 10.0, and the README recommends checking out DNABERT-2 for newer work.

profile.summary: DNABERT-S is a DNA embedding model that turns a DNA sequence into a single vector so that sequences from the same species end up close together. It starts from the DNABERT-2 genome foundation model and is further trained with contrastive learning on pairs of sequences from the same microbial species. The embeddings are meant for tasks such as species clustering, few-shot species classification and metagenomics binning, where many species have no reference genome.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-S starts from the pretrained DNABERT-2 model and continues training it with contrastive learning on pairs of DNA sequences taken from the same species. Training follows a two-phase curriculum (curriculum contrastive learning): first a Weighted SimCLR objective pulls same-species sequences together and pushes different species apart, then a Manifold Instance Mixup (MI-Mix) objective mixes hidden representations at a randomly chosen layer to make harder examples. The resulting embedding, the mean of the last hidden states, can be clustered or fed to a simple classifier to separate species without reference genomes, for example in metagenomics binning.

profile.summary: MP-RNA is an RNA foundation model that reads an RNA sequence one base at a time and produces representations for downstream prediction. It was pretrained on plant transcriptomes from over 1,000 species with objectives that include predicting secondary structure and repairing single-base mutations. It is aimed at tasks that need per-base resolution, such as RNA secondary structure prediction and mutation detection, and the authors also apply it to DNA tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Description, Training Data; paper Section 3

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MP-RNA is a transformer encoder that reads RNA one base at a time. It is pretrained with three combined objectives: masked RNA language modelling, single nucleotide mutation repair (5% of sites are mutated and the model learns to correct them), and secondary structure prediction. Structure labels come from ViennaRNA. To limit noise from these computed labels, the authors keep the 10% of samples with the lowest expected calibration error for incremental pretraining, and append structures to the sequence in 10% of masked language modelling examples. After pretraining, the model is fine-tuned or used for tasks such as secondary structure prediction, mutation detection and repair, and DNA genomic tasks.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility

The paper states that only MP-RNA-186M received incremental pretraining and that the incrementally pretrained 52M model will not be released. Whether any other MP-RNA checkpoint is public was not checked. profile.summary: Omni-DNA is a family of generative DNA language models, named by size from 20M to 1B parameters, that read a DNA sequence and predict the next token. After pretraining on multi-species genomes, a single model can be fine-tuned to answer several tasks at once, producing a class label, a text description of function, or image tokens from a DNA input. The base models can also be fine-tuned with a classification head like other genomic foundation models.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Figure 4; README Capabilities; Hugging Face API

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Omni-DNA works in two stages. First, decoder-only transformers based on OLMo are pretrained on DNA alone by next-token prediction. Then a model is fine-tuned on several tasks at once: the tokenizer vocabulary is expanded with new tokens for each task's outputs (class labels, text, or discrete image codes), and the model learns to generate the answer after the input sequence and a task description. To limit the shift in existing tokens caused by vocabulary expansion, the authors use a method they call Important Key Repetition together with NEFTune. Base models can also be fine-tuned in the usual way with a classification head.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Figure 4, Section 3; README: Capabilities

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Six base sizes and three fine-tuned 1B models are released on Hugging Face. The 116M and 1B models use non-parametric layer norm and the other four use RMSNorm. The repository's run.sh lists the commands used to replicate the paper's experiments, including classification fine-tuning and inference with the multi-task, DNA-to-text and DNA-to-image models. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read Omni-DNA-1B at revision 0ea9d54e.

profile.summary: RiNALMo is an RNA language model that reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and produces a numerical representation of each position. It was pretrained on 36 million non-coding RNA sequences by learning to fill in masked nucleotides, and the representations are then fine-tuned for tasks such as RNA secondary structure prediction and splice site prediction. The largest model has 650M parameters; smaller 148M and 33.5M versions are also released.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RiNALMo is an encoder-only transformer trained by masked language modelling: 15% of tokens in each training sequence are selected, most are replaced with a mask token, and the model learns to reconstruct them. It uses rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU feed-forward layers and FlashAttention-2. Training sequences were sampled once per cluster per epoch to keep batches diverse. For downstream use, the per-nucleotide representations or the classification token embedding feed a task head; the authors fine-tuned it for secondary structure prediction, splice site prediction, mean ribosome loading and ncRNA family classification.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three pretrained sizes are published on Zenodo: giga (650M), mega and micro. Their parameter counts differ slightly between the paper, the README and the Zenodo description. The 650M model was pretrained on seven 80 GB A100 GPUs for 2 weeks. Fine-tuned giga weights and the train_<task>.py scripts allow the paper's downstream evaluations to be rerun. The Python loader in the repository downloads only giga-v1. A result should name the size, whether pretrained or fine-tuned weights were used, and the Zenodo record (15043668).

profile.summary: SpliceBERT is a language model of primary RNA sequence, the full transcript including introns, trained on over 2 million sequences from 72 vertebrates. It reads up to 1024 nucleotides, one token per nucleotide, and outputs an embedding for each position. The authors use it to study RNA splicing: to find splice sites and branchpoints and to score whether a variant is likely to disrupt splicing.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, Methods, Discussion; README introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceBERT is a small BERT model trained by masked language modelling on primary RNA sequences, meaning whole transcripts including introns, from 72 vertebrate genomes. Each nucleotide is one token. The authors use its nucleotide embeddings and attention weights to study splicing: embeddings separate real splice sites from look-alike sites, and a score of how the model's predictions around a variant change (the paper's KL-context score) helps flag splice-disrupting variants. Fine-tuned, it predicts branchpoints and splice sites across species.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One Zenodo archive (record 7995778, version v0.1-alpha) holds three checkpoints that differ in training data and fragment length. The paper pretrained SpliceBERT in two stages, first on fixed 510 nt fragments and then, continuing from that model, on 64 to 1024 nt fragments (7 days on 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, then 3 days on 4); it does not name the released folders. Most analyses in the paper use the vertebrate model and compare it with SpliceBERT-human. The repository has a download script and notebooks for each analysis section, and lists the package versions used (Python 3.9.7, transformers 4.24.0, PyTorch 1.12.1). A result should name the checkpoint folder (SpliceBERT.1024nt, SpliceBERT.510nt or SpliceBERT-human.510nt) and the Zenodo record.

steps.title: Compute embeddings and logits
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
SPLICEBERT_PATH = "/path/to/SpliceBERT/models/model_folder"  # set the path to the folder of pre-trained SpliceBERT
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoModelForTokenClassification

# load tokenizer
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(SPLICEBERT_PATH)

# prepare input sequence
seq = "ACGUACGuacguaCGu"  ## WARNING: this is just a demo. SpliceBERT may not work on sequences shorter than 64nt as it was trained on sequences of 64-1024nt in length
seq = ' '.join(list(seq.upper().replace("U", "T"))) # U -> T and add whitespace
input_ids = tokenizer.encode(seq) # N -> 5, A -> 6, C -> 7, G -> 8, T(U) -> 9. NOTE: a [CLS] and a [SEP] token will be added to the start and the end of seq
input_ids = torch.as_tensor(input_ids) # convert python list to Tensor
input_ids = input_ids.unsqueeze(0) # add batch dimension, shape: (batch_size, sequence_length)

# use huggerface's official API to use SpliceBERT
# get nucleotide embeddings (hidden states)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(SPLICEBERT_PATH) # load model
last_hidden_state = model(input_ids).last_hidden_state # get hidden states from last layer
hiddens_states = model(input_ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states # hidden states from the embedding layer (nn.Embedding) and the 6 transformer encoder layers

# get nucleotide type logits in masked language modeling
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(SPLICEBERT_PATH) # load model
logits = model(input_ids).logits # shape: (batch_size, sequence_length, vocab_size)
PY

profile.summary: GENERator is a family of generative DNA language models that read DNA as six-base tokens and predict what comes next, like a text language model. The models handle long inputs (16,384 tokens, given as 98k base pairs in the first release) and are used to generate DNA sequences, score the effect of variants, and provide embeddings for classification tasks. The first release was trained on 386 billion nucleotides of eukaryotic DNA from RefSeq; the v2 series adds new eukaryote models and prokaryote models, at 1.2B and 3B parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Figure 1 caption, Section 4; v1 card; README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENERator is a decoder-only transformer, built on the LLaMA framework, that predicts the next 6-mer token of a DNA sequence. Grouping six bases per token lets a 16,384-token window cover long stretches of DNA. The authors compared tokenizers for this autoregressive setting and found 6-mers best, with BPE close to random on their sequence recovery test. For the first release they trained only on gene-centric regions of eukaryotic RefSeq genomes rather than whole genomes, which gave lower loss for the whole-genome model but better downstream results for the gene-centric one. Training sequences start at a random offset of 0 to 5 bases so the model sees different 6-mer framings.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2.2.1, 4.1, 4.3

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations. The first release (February 2025) has eukaryote models at 1.2B and 3B parameters. The v2 series (November 2025) adds new eukaryote models and prokaryote models at the same two sizes, described in a separate technical report on bioRxiv. The 1.2B configurations of the first release and v2 are identical; the v2 card adds a per-base sequence scoring function. The README asks users of the prokaryote models to re-download weights updated on 2026-07-06. A result should name the full checkpoint name, including v2 and eukaryote or prokaryote, and its Hugging Face revision. This page read GENERator-v2-eukaryote-1.2b-base at revision c41b0018 and GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base at revision 5e872c94. The paper gives the 1B model's pretraining compute as 11,776 A100-hours (368 hours on 32 GPUs) in Appendix B and as 11,793 A100-hours in its resource table (Table S16); the two figures conflict and the paper does not explain the difference. Table S16 gives 29,625 A100-hours for the 3B model.

steps.title: Generate sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-v2-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    attn_implementation="flash_attention_2",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
).cuda().eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-v2-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

# Define input sequences.
sequences = [
    "ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCG",
    "ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT"
]

# Truncate each sequence to the nearest multiple of 6
processed_sequences = ["<s>" + seq[len(seq)%6:] for seq in sequences]

# Tokenize the sequences
inputs = tokenizer(
    processed_sequences,
    add_special_tokens=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
    padding_side="left",
).to("cuda")

# Generate the sequences
with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=32, do_sample=False)

# Decode the generated sequences
decoded_sequences = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)

# Print the decoded sequences
print(decoded_sequences)
PY

profile.summary: MirrorDNA is a very small DNA language model, 2.35M parameters for the main model, that learns its own way of splitting DNA into tokens. Its tokenizer is built so that a sequence and its reverse complement, the two strands of the same DNA, are always split into mirror-image pieces, so both strands get the same tokens. It is pretrained on the human genome and fine-tuned for DNA classification and regression tasks, giving features that either ignore strand or keep it, depending on the task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening paragraph, Intended use; Hugging Face API

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNA is double-stranded, so the same stretch can be read in either direction as its reverse complement. MirrorDNA learns how to cut a sequence into chunks (its tokens) with a symmetric boundary router built so that a sequence and its reverse complement are always cut into mirror-image chunks, whatever the parameter values. Both strands therefore get the same tokens. Bases pass through an encoder, the router chooses chunk boundaries and a transformer works on the chunks. A decoder produces per-base features at full resolution, from which the model computes its output logits; pretraining is masked language modelling with 15% of bases masked. For downstream tasks the model gives pooled features that do not depend on strand, or orientation-aware features for labels that do, such as promoters or splice sites.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints were released with one pretraining recipe: the main MirrorDNA model, a duplex-encoder variant, and a control without the equivariance guarantee that relies on reverse-complement augmentation instead. The repository includes the weights, a numerical test of the equivariance guarantee, a two-minute quick start on a small test data set, and scripts to rerun every pretraining, baseline and analysis step of the paper. A result should name the checkpoint folder or Hugging Face repository and its revision; this page read the repository at commit 9c432fc4 and mirrordna-tiny on Hugging Face at revision 11bedeae.

facts.value: An encoder over bases (shared-weight convolutional in MirrorDNA, cross-strand gated duplex in MirrorDNA-duplex), a symmetric boundary router that cuts the sequence into chunks, a chunk transformer, a decoder and task heads.
